evidence.claim: An inland freeway through valleys and over the Sunol Grade
evidence.quote: The highway crosses over Mission Pass, also known as the Sunol Grade, and descends into the Sunol Valley

evidence.claim: Interstate 680 crosses Alameda County through Coast Range hills and valleys, climbing over Mission Pass, also called the Sunol Grade.
evidence.quote: enters the hills and valleys of the California Coast Ranges. The highway crosses over Mission Pass, also known as the Sunol Grade

evidence.claim: Its scenic section extends from Mission Boulevard in Fremont to the Contra Costa county line.
evidence.quote: is only a scenic route from Mission Boulevard to the Contra Costa county line

evidence.claim: That status recognizes a landscape meeting the state scenic-highway standard of memorable scenery without visual intrusions.
evidence.quote: this means that those portions are substantial sections of highway passing through a "memorable landscape" with no "visual intrusions"

evidence.claim: The freeway follows a much older corridor. By the 1920s, a road connected Dublin and Sunol with Mission San Jose, but the section south of Dublin was still unpaved.
evidence.quote: By the 1920s, a road ran south from Martinez through Walnut Creek, Dublin, Danville, and Sunol to Mission San Jose

evidence.claim: Most of the road entered the state system in 1933. By 1937 it carried the SR 21 number.
evidence.quote: The majority of this roadway was added to the state highway system in 1933

evidence.claim: In 1955, the Bureau of Public Roads approved a Bay Area interstate loop whose eastern half became I-680.
evidence.quote: The Bureau of Public Roads approved urban routes of the Interstate Highway System on September 15, 1955, including a loop around the San Francisco Bay, soon numbered I-280 and I-680.

evidence.claim: the section south of Dublin was still unpaved.
evidence.quote: It was not yet paved south of Dublin

evidence.claim: By 1937 it carried the SR 21 number.
evidence.quote: by 1937, they had been numbered SR 21.

evidence.claim: Traveling south from the county line, pass through Dublin and the I-580 interchange, then Pleasanton, before reaching the Sunol Valley.
evidence.quote: Afterward, it enters Pleasanton and intersects with I-580, currently California's longest auxiliary Interstate providing access to Oakland and the Central Valley. It enters Dublin for a short segment before exiting the county and entering Contra Costa County.

evidence.claim: Near Sunol the freeway shares a short stretch with SR 84. From the valley it crosses Mission Pass and turns toward Fremont and Mission Boulevard, completing the scenic section.
evidence.quote: Continuing through the city, it meets Mission Boulevard at SR 238 before exiting the city. Prior to 2002, two ghost ramps existed here, remains of an abandoned freeway project replacing Mission Boulevard. Amid Alameda County, it abruptly turns northeastward and enters a hilly area, where it crosses over Mission Pass, and descends into the Sunol Valley, where it runs concurrently with SR 84 for a short while.

evidence.claim: Pleasanton’s earlier settlement, Alisal, formed near the Francisco Solano Alviso Adobe, built in 1844. The adobe survives as the centerpiece of Alviso Adobe Community Park.
evidence.quote: around the Francisco Solano Alviso Adobe called El Alisal (The Sycamores), one of the earliest houses built in the valley in 1844. It is still standing and serves as the centerpiece of the Alviso Adobe Community Park.

evidence.claim: After World War II, farming and ranching gave way to a commuter community and corporate headquarters as the Bay Area grew.
evidence.quote: After World War II, Pleasanton changed from being primarily focused on farming and ranching to being a bedroom community and a place for corporate headquarters due to major growth of the Bay Area.

evidence.claim: Downtown preserves another part of that changing town: Gothic Revival, Italianate and Queen Anne buildings stand within walking distance of one another. A Main Street redesign in the 1990s emphasized pedestrians and outdoor dining.
evidence.quote: Buildings in Gothic Revival, Pioneer, Italianate, Commercial Italianate, Colonial Revival, and Queen Anne styles can be found within walking distance of each other.

evidence.claim: Pleasanton’s earlier settlement, Alisal
evidence.quote: Before the establishment of Pleasanton in the 1850s, an earlier settlement in the location was called Alisal.

evidence.claim: A Main Street redesign in the 1990s emphasized pedestrians and outdoor dining.
evidence.quote: A redesign of Main Street in the 1990s emphasized pedestrian traffic and outdoor dining.

evidence.claim: Sunol’s 1884 depot combined passenger, freight and station-agent facilities under one roof. It is the last surviving example of Southern Pacific’s standard No. 7 design.
evidence.quote: This one-story Stick style depot was built to Southern Pacific standard design No. 7 in 1884.

evidence.claim: The agent’s office has a five-window bay facing the tracks, while the freight room’s raised floor matched the height of freight cars and wagons.
evidence.quote: The agents office is next to the west and features a five-window bay on the track side

evidence.claim: After Southern Pacific ended canyon operations in 1984, the Pacific Locomotive Association began rebuilding track in 1987. The first Niles Canyon Railway passenger train left Sunol in May 1988.
evidence.quote: Southern Pacific ceased its operations through the canyon in 1984

evidence.claim: The depot’s freight room now serves exhibits and meetings.
evidence.quote: This room is now used for exhibits and meetings.

evidence.claim: combined passenger, freight and station-agent facilities under one roof.
evidence.quote: A “combination depot” such as this housed facilities for a company agent, freight and passengers in one building

evidence.claim: It is the last surviving example of Southern Pacific’s standard No. 7 design.
evidence.quote: Out of at least eleven No. 7 depots built by the railroad, Sunol is the last one remaining.

evidence.claim: the freight room’s raised floor matched the height of freight cars and wagons.
evidence.quote: the freight room takes up the rest of the building and is set about forty inches above grade so that its floor would be level with the floor of freight cars and teamsters’ wagons.

evidence.claim: the Pacific Locomotive Association began rebuilding track in 1987. The first Niles Canyon Railway passenger train left Sunol in May 1988.
evidence.quote: The Pacific Locomotive Association leased the right of way from the county and began working to reconstruct the track in 1987. The Niles Canyon Railway ran its first passenger train from Sunol on May 21, 1988.

evidence.claim: Twelve concrete Corinthian columns make a water junction into a classical pavilion. Willis Polk designed the Sunol Water Temple, built in 1910, after the Temple of Vesta at Tivoli.
evidence.quote: Designed by Willis Polk, the 59-foot (18 m) high classical pavilion is made up of twelve concrete Corinthian columns

evidence.claim: It marked the meeting of three underground water sources. Before the Hetch Hetchy Aqueduct was built, half of San Francisco’s water supply passed through it.
evidence.quote: Prior to the construction of the Hetch Hetchy Aqueduct, half of San Francisco's water supply (6,000,000 US gallons (23,000,000 L; 5,000,000 imp gal) a day) passed through the Sunol temple.

evidence.claim: The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake severely damaged the deteriorating structure. Restoration from 1997 to 2001 added seismic and accessibility improvements. Water flowing through the temple is no longer part of the drinking-water supply.
evidence.quote: A community effort led to the temple's restoration from 1997 to 2001, at a cost of $1.2 million, including seismic and accessibility upgrades.

evidence.claim: Willis Polk designed the Sunol Water Temple, built in 1910, after the Temple of Vesta at Tivoli.
evidence.quote: Polk's design, modeled after the ancient Temple of Vesta in Tivoli, Italy, was constructed in 1910

evidence.claim: It marked the meeting of three underground water sources.
evidence.quote: atop the spot where three subterranean water sources converge

evidence.claim: The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake severely damaged the deteriorating structure.
evidence.quote: By the 1980s the water temple had badly deteriorated, and was severely damaged in 1989's Loma Prieta earthquake

evidence.claim: Water flowing through the temple is no longer part of the drinking-water supply.
evidence.quote: Today any water that flows through the temple is not part of the potable water supply.

evidence.claim: The Sunol Valley remains largely rural despite its proximity to Fremont, Pleasanton and Livermore. The freeway runs through this valley before crossing the pass, a gap in the Mount Hamilton Range.
evidence.quote: It is largely rural, but is in proximity to the highly populated Bay Area suburbs of Fremont, Pleasanton, and Livermore.

evidence.claim: The freeway runs through this valley before crossing the pass, a gap in the Mount Hamilton Range.
evidence.quote: Mission Pass, also known as the Sunol Grade and formerly as Stockton Pass, is a gap in the hills of the Mount Hamilton Range in Alameda County, California.

evidence.claim: The freeway runs through this valley
evidence.quote: Interstate 680 runs through the valley.

evidence.claim: During the 1960s, freeway construction reached south to Mission San Jose.
evidence.quote: In the next decade, the freeway was completed from Vallejo south to SR 238 at Mission San Jose

evidence.claim: Alisal Elementary School preserves the earlier settlement’s name, another link to the town that preceded Pleasanton.
evidence.quote: Alisal Elementary School reflects the city's original name.

evidence.claim: Its roof pairs a gabled section over the eastern rooms with a higher hipped section over the freight room.
evidence.quote: The roof is divided into two parts with a gable roof over the east end, and an elevated hip roof over the freight room to the west.

evidence.claim: San Francisco purchased the Spring Valley Water Company, including the temple, in 1930.
evidence.quote: The SVWC, including the temple, was purchased by San Francisco in 1930 for $40 million.
